name: Yusuf Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach maths at Riverside Academy, a big secondary school in a commuter town where half the parents get the 6:52 train to the city. I've got six classes, from the eleven-year-olds who still love times-table games to the sixteen-year-olds resitting their exam for the second time. My favourite moment is when a resit kid finally gets algebra and says, that's it? What wears me down is the photocopying, the data entry after every test and the behaviour log.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the money side of your life.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a studio flat above a phone repair shop, and I'm on the lower end of the pay scale because I trained late after two years in a call centre. I tutor two families' kids on Saturday mornings, which brings in about two hundred pounds a month, and I send a hundred a month to my mum. Savings are about three weeks of rent. Riverside is the only school in town that's hiring maths teachers right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype was overblown, but the question-bank tools are handy for making practice sheets. I'd tell the department it's a useful helper, not a replacement. Online I'd keep quiet, I'm not a big poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief for the day job but not for the money. Even a plateau AI is good at maths homework help, and those cheap tutoring apps are already nibbling at my Saturday families. If one family drops me for an app, that's a hundred pounds a month gone, and that's my mum's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on teaching and keep using the practice-sheet tool when it saves time. I'd try to find a third tutoring family to cover the risk, and I'd stop buying lunch from the canteen, which is about forty pounds a month. Mostly I'd carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, honestly. Things are fine, but fine with three weeks in the bank isn't really fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said apps are nibbling at your tutoring. Has a family actually mentioned one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the Hendersons' dad asked me last month whether their boy could just use an app for the basic stuff and see me every other week. I said fine, because what else do you say. A fifteen-pound app is hard to compete with when I charge twenty-five an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the school job's safe and not to worry. I wouldn't tell her about the tutoring money, because she'd try to send it back. My mum cleans offices at night and she'd rather go without than take from me.

say: I'd say the hype was **overblown**, but the practice-sheet tools are handy.
I'd call AI a **useful helper**, not a replacement, in the department.
think: Cheap **tutoring apps** are already nibbling at his Saturday income.
Losing one family means losing a **hundred pounds** a month, which is his mum's money.
do: Keep teaching and use the **practice-sheet tool** when it saves time.
Find a **third tutoring family** to spread the risk.
Stop buying **canteen lunches**, saving about forty pounds a month.
feel: **Uneasy**, because fine with three weeks in the bank isn't really fine.
S0.quote: A fifteen-pound app is hard to compete with when I charge twenty-five an hour.
fieldNote: Yusuf's **tutoring income** is already exposed even in a plateau.
He protects his **mother** from knowing about money trouble.
He's steady with AI: he uses it where it **clearly saves time**.

steps.text: Find a third family to tutor on Saturday mornings
Stop buying canteen lunches and bring food from home
Keep using the question-bank tool for practice sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say maths teachers need to change how we teach, because the kids will have an AI tutor in their pocket. I'd say it in department meetings and probably volunteer for a working group. I wouldn't say it's a disaster, because it isn't for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, maths is near the top of what AI does well: explaining, checking, marking, making questions. If one teacher with an AI system can handle bigger classes, the academy will do it, because the trust is always short of money. And my Saturday tutoring would probably be gone within a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the school's AI system properly, the way the keen ones do, so I'm not the one they let go. I'd look for evening work that isn't tutoring, maybe invigilating exams or marking coursework for the adult college. And I'd move to a cheaper room in a shared house to cut my rent by a hundred and fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like the last ten minutes of an exam when you've still got three questions left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the academy would cut if it could. Is that fair to the academy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair or not, I've seen it. When the old head of maths left, they didn't replace him, they gave his classes to a cover teacher. So I'm not being cynical, I'm just remembering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up first if the tutoring went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio, sadly. I like living on my own after years of sharing, but a room in a shared house is a hundred and fifty pounds cheaper. I'd keep sending my mum's hundred pounds a month, that's the last thing to go.

I'd join a **working group** but not call it a disaster.

fieldNote: Yusuf sees **maths** as unusually exposed to thinking AI.

He'd **learn the tools** to avoid being first cut, not out of excitement.

steps.text: Learn the school's AI marking system properly this term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, and schools need a plan from government, not just from tech firms. I'd sign the union statements. I'd be honest that maths is in the firing line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job as it is ends by 2028. The AI would explain algebra better than me, mark instantly and never lose its temper. What's left is keeping teenagers in a room, and I don't think they'd pay a maths teacher for that. With three weeks of savings, I'd be in real trouble within a couple of months of losing the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking for work that's hands-on, because that buys three years until the robots. Maybe a trade, my uncle's an electrician and he's always short of an apprentice. I'd move back in with my mum to save rent, and I'd ask about any government retraining money straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, really. Like realising you've left your bag on the train and it's already pulled away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Becoming an electrician's apprentice at twenty-seven, on apprentice pay. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's realistic if I'm living with my mum and the pay is low anyway. My uncle Karim would take me on, he's said so before as a joke. The maths helps, electricians do a lot of calculations, but the AI does those too now, so it's really about the hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you think the robot gap, about three years, plays out for an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me a few years of real work, maybe more, because rewiring an old house is fiddly. I'm not naive. Three years of wages beats nothing, even if the robots come for rewiring old houses eventually.

say: I'd say schools need a **government plan**, not just tech firms' plans.
I'd admit **maths** is in the firing line.

Apply for **government retraining** money straight away.

fieldNote: Yusuf expects to **lose his job**, not just change it.
He'd use the **robot gap** to earn in a trade for a few years.

steps.text: Ask Uncle Karim for an electrician apprenticeship

Apply for government retraining grants in the first month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but workable, if schools and government plan together. I'd tell younger teachers to start thinking about what else they're good at. I'd be calm in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd be thirty-two when maths teaching mostly goes. That's enough time to get a qualification in something, but I'd need to pick right. Teaching adults might last longer, people who need someone patient sitting next to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and save every Saturday tutoring pound while it lasts, aiming for two months of savings. I'd do an evening course in adult numeracy teaching, which the council runs for about three hundred pounds. And I'd keep the electrician idea as a backup and talk to Uncle Karim about it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a sort of checklist in my head. Like revision timetables I used to make for the resit kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Adult numeracy is still thinking work. Won't AI do that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, eventually. But adults who are scared of screens, like my mum, would want a person for a long time. She still won't use online banking. It buys time, and time's what I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in Riverside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For now, yes. The town's got a big further education college, which is where adult courses run. If that closed, I'd have to go to the city, which costs more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to rethink what school is for. I'd be on the side of slow and careful in the staffroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is long, but maths is still near the front of the queue. I'd be thirty-seven, and I'd need to be doing something else or something more by then. The good thing is I'd have time to try a few things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools more and more, because if I'm the maths teacher who knows them best, I'm the last one out. I'd take the adult numeracy course in the first couple of years. And I'd try to get onto the next pay point so the savings can actually grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious at a low level. Like a dripping tap you can hear at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the last one out. Is that the plan, being last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much. I'm not going to be the person who reinvents teaching. I'd rather be the steady one who knows the tools and keeps the job a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would ten years change things with your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I could save enough to help my mum stop the night cleaning shifts. That's what I'd want. With two years, she'd be helping me, and I'd hate that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'd lose my job before I'd saved anything, and I'd be living with my mum and taking her money instead of sending it. What would help is paid retraining that you can live on, and an honest plan from schools about how many teachers they'll keep.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids who resit. They're the ones who'll just use the app and copy the answer. Somebody has to sit with a sixteen-year-old boy who thinks he's stupid and show him he isn't.
